title: Community grants program review discussion
subtitle: Tier 1 funding, in-kind facility grants, equity funds and transparency discussed; no recommendations yet, closed session followed.
overview: Council held a special meeting to discuss an external review of the City's Community Grants Program. The item was for discussion and feedback only. Staff said they have no recommendations yet and will return after a second round of community engagement this fall.

The review found that the program gives groups steady support. It also found problems: the Tier 2 application is long, evaluation criteria are unclear, the program is not tied to current strategic priorities, and Tier 1 funding is not competitive and not open to new applicants. Staff outlined best practices used elsewhere, including shorter forms, themed funding, competitive multi-year funding and replacing in-kind facility grants with cash.
Councillors asked staff to include the Love My Hood and RISE programs when the item returns. They also asked for clearer public reporting on how grant money is used.
The only formal vote was to hold a closed session after the meeting on a possible land disposition and a legal advice matter {{vote:m1}}. The minutes report no further decisions.

decisions.detail: Council agreed to meet in closed session after the special meeting to consider a potential land disposition and a matter of solicitor-client privilege, the only formal motion of the meeting {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Staff and the consultant said 85% of grant funding goes to Tier 1 groups without competition, leaving a small competitive pool for Tier 2. They said this puts newer and grassroots groups at a disadvantage and is unlike peer municipalities.

Several councillors said Love My Hood and RISE should be part of the picture. One said that adding them would put Kitchener well above peer averages and could change how equity is weighed in Tier 2. Staff replied that the review covered only the original program and that peers' equity funds would also need to be counted for a fair comparison.

Some councillors were cautious about changing a program that has run without major complaints. They worried about 'best practices' from other cities and wanted accountability kept, with a form shorter than now but not too short. One councillor noted that a published scoring rubric might lead to more appeals.

On in-kind grants, staff said facility access is harder as programming grows, and cash would let groups choose venues. Some councillors worried about losing park fee waivers and about revenue shortfalls at City facilities, and suggested a pilot or a priority for City venues.

Councillors supported public reporting of funded groups and of community outcomes each year, and updating priorities each term of Council. One suggested holding back some money for opportunities that arise after the deadline. The Mayor was unsure about fixed funding categories.
